source_refs.note: Exercise 12.2, Question 2 (i)-(ii): continuity of piecewise functions at x = c (book p.233). Answer key PDF 310 wrongly says (i) is discontinuous at x = 2.

blocks.prompt: 2 (i) Discuss the continuity of \(f(x)\) at \(x = c\): \[f(x) = \begin{cases} 2x + 5, & x \le 2 \\ 4x + 1, & x > 2 \end{cases}\]\(c = 2\)
blocks.explanation:
A continuity question for a two-piece function.
We must decide whether \(f\) is continuous at \(x = 2\), where the formula changes.
Plan: find \(f(2)\), the LHL and the RHL, then test the three conditions.
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = 2x + 5\) for \(x \le 2\), \(4x + 1\) for \(x > 2\); \(c = 2\).
To find: whether \(f\) is continuous at \(x = 2\).
Method: \(f\) is continuous at \(x = c\) when three conditions hold: (i) \(f(c)\) is defined, (ii) \(\lim_{x \to c} f(x)\) exists (LHL = RHL), (iii) \(\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)\). If any one fails, \(f\) is discontinuous at \(c\).

Condition (i): find \(f(2)\)
\[f(2) = 2(2) + 5 = 9\]
Why: The sign \(\le\) puts \(x = 2\) in the first piece \(2x + 5\).

Left hand limit
\[\lim_{x \to 2^-} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 2^-} (2x + 5)\]
\[= 4 + 5 = 9\]
Why: For \(x < 2\) the first piece is used.

Right hand limit
\[\lim_{x \to 2^+} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 2^+} (4x + 1)\]
\[= 8 + 1 = 9\]
Why: For \(x > 2\) the second piece is used.

Condition (ii): does the limit exist?
\[\text{LHL} = \text{RHL} = 9\]
\[\lim_{x \to 2} f(x) = 9\]
Why: The one-sided limits are equal.

Condition (iii): compare with \(f(2)\)
\[\lim_{x \to 2} f(x) = 9 = f(2)\]
Why: All three conditions hold, so the two straight-line pieces meet at the same point \((2, 9)\): no break.

Check
\[f(1.99) = 3.98 + 5 = 8.98\]
\[f(2.01) = 8.04 + 1 = 9.04\]
Why: Values on both sides are close to \(f(2) = 9\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key prints "(i) \(f\) is discontinuous at \(x = 2\)". This is wrong: \(f(2) = 9\), the left hand limit is \(2(2) + 5 = 9\) and the right hand limit is \(4(2) + 1 = 9\), so all three conditions hold. The correct answer is: \(f\) is continuous at \(x = 2\).

blocks.prompt: 2 (ii) Discuss the continuity of \(f(x)\) at \(x = c\): \[f(x) = \begin{cases} 3x - 1, & x < 1 \\ 4, & x = 1 \\ 2x, & x > 1 \end{cases}\]\(c = 1\)
blocks.explanation:
A continuity question for a three-piece function: one formula on each side and a separate value at the point.
We must decide whether \(f\) is continuous at \(x = 1\).
Plan: find \(f(1)\), the LHL and the RHL, then test the three conditions.
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = 3x - 1\) for \(x < 1\), \(f(1) = 4\), \(f(x) = 2x\) for \(x > 1\); \(c = 1\).
To find: whether \(f\) is continuous at \(x = 1\).
Method: \(f\) is continuous at \(x = c\) when three conditions hold: (i) \(f(c)\) is defined, (ii) \(\lim_{x \to c} f(x)\) exists (LHL = RHL), (iii) \(\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)\). If any one fails, \(f\) is discontinuous at \(c\).

Condition (i): find \(f(1)\)
\[f(1) = 4\]
Why: The middle line gives the value at exactly \(x = 1\).

Left hand limit
\[\lim_{x \to 1^-} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 1^-} (3x - 1)\]
\[= 3 - 1 = 2\]
Why: For \(x < 1\) the first piece is used.

Right hand limit
\[\lim_{x \to 1^+} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 1^+} 2x\]
\[= 2(1) = 2\]
Why: For \(x > 1\) the third piece is used.

Condition (ii): does the limit exist?
\[\text{LHL} = \text{RHL} = 2\]
\[\lim_{x \to 1} f(x) = 2\]
Why: The one-sided limits are equal, so the limit exists.

Condition (iii): compare with \(f(1)\)
\[\lim_{x \to 1} f(x) = 2\]
\[f(1) = 4\]
\[2 \ne 4\]
Why: The limit does not equal the value of the function, so condition (iii) fails. The graph approaches the point \((1, 2)\) but the function's point is \((1, 4)\): a hole in the line with a separate dot above it.

Check
\[f(0.99) = 2.97 - 1 = 1.97\]
\[f(1.01) = 2.02\]
Why: Nearby values approach 2, not 4. (If \(f(1)\) were 2, \(f\) would be continuous.)
blocks.final_answer: \(f\) is discontinuous at \(x = 1\) (the limit is 2 but \(f(1) = 4\))
